title: Cashless Bail Reporting Act
official_title: To direct the Attorney General to make publicly available a list of each State and unit of local government that permits cashless bail, and for other purposes.
summary: The Attorney General must publish a list of every state and local government that allows defendants charged with a “covered offense” (a crime the Attorney General determines poses a clear threat to public safety and order) to be released before trial without posting cash — either on personal recognizance or an unsecured appearance bond. The list must go up within one year of enactment and be updated annually.
brief: Directs the Attorney General to publish and annually update a public list of jurisdictions that permit pretrial release on personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond.

top_lines.headline: Attorney General Publication Requirement
subs: Published list must identify every state and local government permitting a person charged with a covered offense to be released on personal recognizance or unsecured bond
Initial publication required within one year of enactment; updated on an annual basis

likelihoodReason: The bill passed the House 308-116 — a margin indicating substantial Democratic crossover support, with roughly 80+ Democrats voting yes alongside the Republican majority. This bipartisan House coalition improves Senate prospects, but 60 Senate votes are still required to clear a filibuster. Cashless bail policy divides Senate Democrats, and no companion Senate bill has been identified. The crossover strength in the House is encouraging but not determinative.

items.main: Names the Act the “Cashless Bail Reporting Act”.
items.detail: Short-title section — citation name only; no substantive effect.

sections.label: Section 2 — Publication of Cashless Bail Jurisdictions

items.main: The Attorney General must make publicly available a list of each state and unit of local government that permits pretrial release of a person charged with a covered offense on personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond within one year of enactment, updated annually.
items.detail: The list is limited to jurisdictions that permit such release for a person charged with a “covered offense” — defined in subsection (b) as a criminal offense the Attorney General determines poses a clear threat to public safety and order, including violent or sexual acts (murder, rape, sexual assault, carjacking, robbery, burglary, assault) and offenses that promote public disorder (looting, vandalism, destruction of property, rioting or inciting to riot, fleeing a law enforcement officer). No format, publication platform, or enforcement mechanism for failure to update is specified in the bill text.

underreported.summary: The list only covers jurisdictions that permit release for a "covered offense" — a term the bill leaves substantially to the Attorney General's discretion, defined as any offense the AG determines "poses a clear threat to public safety and order." The enumerated crimes (murder, rape, assault, looting, rioting, etc.) are introduced by "including," making the list illustrative rather than exhaustive.
underreported.why_unreported: Because the offense list is non-exhaustive, the Attorney General has discretion to expand which offenses qualify as "covered" beyond the named crimes — meaning the scope of jurisdictions captured on the published list is not fixed by the statute itself but depends on the AG's ongoing determination of what poses a public-safety threat.

criticisms.why: today, I rise in support of my bill, H.R. 5625, the Cashless Bail Reporting Act. In August of 2025, the whole Nation watched in horror as we witnessed the brutal murder of Ukrainian refugee Iryna Zarutska on a Charlotte light rail. This murder took place right outside my district in a city I have called home for many years. This tragic incident cannot be described as anything other than a cold-blooded murder carried out by a dangerous individual who should not have been out on the streets to begin with.

gaps: The bill requires annual publication of the list but specifies no format, accessibility standard, or enforcement mechanism for failure to publish or update.

The bill covers release on personal recognizance and unsecured appearance bonds but does not address other low- or no-cash release mechanisms — property bonds, electronic monitoring conditions, or supervised release programs — that are not captured by the reporting requirement.

added: Requirement for Attorney General to publicly list all states and local governments permitting pretrial release of persons charged with a covered offense on personal recognizance or unsecured appearance bond, published within one year and updated annually

New "covered offense" definition: a crime the Attorney General finds poses a clear threat to public safety, including violent/sexual acts (murder, rape, sexual assault, carjacking, robbery, burglary, assault) and public-disorder offenses (looting, vandalism, destruction of property, rioting/inciting to riot, fleeing a law enforcement officer)
modified: Publication deadline lengthened from "not later than 30 days" to "not later than one year" after enactment
Update frequency changed from quarterly to annually
List scope narrowed from jurisdictions that release any person "charged with an offense" to only those charged with a "covered offense"
